title: Asteria Health - Private VPC Discovery
summary: Initial discovery focused on private/VPC deployment options for Redwood Private. Customer has strict data residency and network isolation requirements, is evaluating VPC peering vs PrivateLink/transit gateway, and needs guidance on cross-account connectivity, DNS, and KMS integration. Agreed next steps: share network diagram, security docs, SSO/KMS details, schedule technical deep dive to run benchmark and pilot scope.
topics: VPC peering vs PrivateLink vs Transit Gateway
Egress rules, NAT, and security groups
Pilot scope and success criteria (latency, throughput)
next_steps: Redwood: share Private deployment network guide + sample VPC diagram
Asteria: send current VPC CIDRs and peering/topology docs
Schedule SE deep-dive and benchmark run week of 2026-05-25
Redwood: share SOC2 and KMS/HSM integration docs
action_items: Rob Patel - Provide VPC CIDR ranges, account IDs, and current peering topology - due 2026-05-20
Jordan Lee - Draft proposed network architecture options (peering, PrivateLink, Transit GW) - due 2026-05-19
Maya Chen - Send pricing range and pilot contract template - due 2026-05-18

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-15
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~54 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Jordan Lee (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (CTO - Asteria), Rob Patel (Head Infra), Emily Nguyen (Security), Samir Das (ML Platform)

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya, AE for Redwood, and with me is Jordan our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:10] Lena Ortiz: Doing well, thanks. Busy week but excited to get into the network stuff, this is our main blocker right now.
[00:16] Rob Patel: Yeah, hi, Rob here. We want to make sure we can put Redwood in our private VPC without opening egress to the public internet.
[00:22] Jordan Lee: Great, that's exactly what we typically do for Private deployments. Today we can talk through VPC peering, AWS PrivateLink, transit gateway, DNS, and KMS/HSM integration.
[00:33] Emily Nguyen: Quick note from security side: we need SOC 2 controls, full audit logs, customer-managed keys, and proof we can avoid any cross-account data egress to public endpoints.
[00:44] Maya Chen: Totally understood. High level, Redwood Private offers a private control plane with customer-managed networking. You can run the inference nodes in your AWS account or we can run them in a dedicated account with VPC peering or PrivateLink to your VPC.
[00:58] Samir Das: Can you clarify the account model? We prefer everything in our account for control, but if there's a managed option that's acceptable as long as the network is private.
[01:10] Jordan Lee: Sure. Option A: customer-hosted nodes in your account—Redwood provides AMIs/container images and orchestration manifests; you manage the VPC, subnets, and security groups. Option B: Redwood-hosted in a dedicated AWS account with VPC peering or PrivateLink to your VPC, which gives us operational control but keeps network traffic internal.
[01:33] Lena Ortiz: What about peering limits? We have multiple business units, and we don't want to create a peering mesh that blows up.
[01:40] Jordan Lee: Good question. Peering scales but it's point-to-point and can be cumbersome with many accounts. For multi-account setups we recommend Transit Gateway or PrivateLink behind an NLB. Transit GW is typically our recommendation for larger orgs; PrivateLink is good for strict private endpoints per service.
[01:56] Rob Patel: Transit Gateway might be better. We already have a TGW in us-east-1 and eu-west-1. Does Redwood attach to a TGW or do we need a dedicated attachment?
[02:06] Jordan Lee: We can attach to your TGW. We usually propose a VPC attachment from our deployment VPC to your TGW, or you create an attachment from your side depending on account ownership. We'll share example CloudFormation/IaC snippets.
[02:20] Maya Chen: Also want to call out DNS — split-horizon DNS is common: you need private hosted zones for the endpoints so internal names resolve to private IPs. We'll provide guidance for Route 53 private zones or on-prem DNS forwarders.
[02:35] Emily Nguyen: About DNS, we run strict split-horizon and want mutual TLS between our services and the inference endpoints. Can Redwood support mTLS and client certs?
[02:44] Jordan Lee: Yes, we support mTLS for service-to-service traffic and you can configure mutual TLS on the NLB/ALB in front of the private endpoint. For control plane we support SAML SSO and RBAC, and we can integrate with your IdP.
[02:59] Samir Das: Latency is also a concern — our app expects p95 generation latency under 200ms for short prompts. With private hosting in the same region should be fine, but we need to validate.
[03:10] Jordan Lee: Right, region and instance size matter. If you colocate the inference nodes in the same AZs as your app frontends and route via private endpoints, you should see very low network latency. Our standard recommendations will include instance families and batching configs for low-latency workloads.
[03:28] Lena Ortiz: We have strict data residency constraints. The initial scope is EU workloads in eu-west-1 only. We cannot have any inference traffic leave eu-west-1. Is Redwood able to guarantee region restriction?
[03:39] Jordan Lee: Yes, we can pin deployments to specific regions. For Redwood-hosted accounts we provision in the requested region. For customer-hosted, it's your VPC so it's already regional. We'll include region pinning in the pilot SLAs.
[03:52] Rob Patel: On the topic of keys, we use AWS KMS with customer-managed CMKs and require that any platform doing encryption-at-rest use our keys via cross-account grants. How does Redwood handle KMS integration when we host nodes in our account vs Redwood-hosted?
[04:04] Jordan Lee: If nodes are in your account you control the KMS keys directly. For Redwood-hosted nodes, we support envelope encryption with customer-managed keys via cross-account roles and grants. There's a small additional ops step to configure key policies, and we'll share documentation on the required grants.
[04:20] Emily Nguyen: Do you support HSM-backed keys (CloudHSM) or external HSM? We have a few regulated datasets that require key material in an HSM.
[04:29] Jordan Lee: We integrate with CloudHSM via customer-managed keys and can discuss a custom HSM setup for Private/On-prem deployments. There is usually a security review for that path.
[04:38] Maya Chen: We should probably schedule a security deep-dive after you share your compliance checklist. Emily, is it okay if we send SOC 2 docs and the KMS guide?
[04:45] Emily Nguyen: Yes, please send SOC2 and any pen test summaries, and also list of encryption algorithms used, TLS versions, and cert rotation details.
[04:54] Maya Chen: Will do.
[05:00] Jordan Lee: Moving back to networking — another common gotcha is overlapping CIDRs. If your VPC CIDR overlaps with our deployment VPC, peering and routing won't work. We need your CIDR ranges to plan.
[05:11] Rob Patel: We'll share CIDRs. We have a few /16s and some AZ-specific /24s in the app VPCs.
[05:18] Samir Das: For the first pilot we want minimal scope: one inference cluster in eu-west-1, connected to our app VPC via TGW, run benchmarks with 100 concurrent requests of small prompts, measure p95 and token throughput. If that passes, we expand.
[05:33] Jordan Lee: That sounds reasonable. For benchmarking we'll want sample prompts and expected token lengths. We can run both real-time and batch tests and provide token-level cost estimates.
[05:42] Lena Ortiz: Regarding observability, we need per-request audit logs and traceability back to user IDs. How granular are logs from Redwood Private?
[05:50] Jordan Lee: We can emit request/response metadata to your logging endpoint (CloudWatch/Elastic/Kinesis). For privacy we can redact content but still provide request IDs, model version, token counts, latency, and error traces.
[06:02] Emily Nguyen: And retention? We default to 30 days, but we need options for 90/365 for compliance purposes.
[06:08] Jordan Lee: Retention is configurable in Private. We'll include retention options in the docs.
[06:14] Maya Chen: Any concerns around egress? If the inference nodes need to pull model shards or updates from Redwood, will that hit the public internet?
[06:22] Jordan Lee: For customer-hosted nodes you pull model artifacts from a signed S3 endpoint we provide — you can set up VPC endpoints (Gateway S3 endpoints) so traffic never leaves AWS backbone. For Redwood-hosted nodes we can publish artifacts into an S3 bucket in your account or use a private transfer mechanism.
[06:38] Rob Patel: That's good. How much control do we have over AMI/container images? We require image scanning and FIPS-compatible libraries on some nodes.
[06:46] Jordan Lee: You can bring your own images if you self-host. We also provide hardened images and can work with your security team for image scanning and FIPS builds.
[06:54] Lena Ortiz: Are there available compliance attestations for Redwood Private?
[06:58] Maya Chen: Yes, we have SOC 2 Type II and some customers have completed specific security assessments. We'll share the security pack. For healthcare workloads we also have HIPAA guidance — we can discuss BAAs with legal if needed.
[07:12] Samir Das: One implementation detail — how does model version pinning and rollout work in Private? We need predictable rollouts and the ability to quickly rollback if a model causes regressions.
[07:22] Jordan Lee: In Private, you control the rollout policy. We provide the control plane API to pin model versions, create canary groups, and set automatic fallback. Rollbacks are a single API call. If you need we can run a canary in a subset of pods behind a weight-based router.
[07:35] Rob Patel: Network ACLs — do you need specific ephemeral port ranges opened between our app subnets and the inference subnets? We're strict on allowed ports.
[07:43] Jordan Lee: Communication is over HTTPS typically, plus any internal service ports for health checks. We'll provide a minimal port list and health check endpoints. If you enforce NACLs we recommend whitelisting the NLB/ENI IP ranges that we provide during setup.
[07:58] Emily Nguyen: How do you handle identity for the control plane actions? We require that API actions are tied to our SSO identities and we can map roles to Redwood roles.
[08:06] Jordan Lee: We support SAML 2.0 SSO and SCIM provisioning; you can map your IdP groups to Redwood roles and enforce MFA. Audit logs will show the IdP user events.
[08:18] Maya Chen: It's sounding like we have clear steps. Rob, can you share CIDRs and TGW attachment contact? Emily, any other compliance items to flag now?
[08:28] Emily Nguyen: Please include the pen test summary, a network architecture reference with expected IP ranges, and a BAA template if you have one.
[08:36] Maya Chen: We'll collect those.
[08:39] Jordan Lee: Quick note on limits — if you expect very high QPS, we might recommend Dedicated reserved capacity with pinned GPUs for throughput predictability. For the pilot we'll size to your expected concurrency.
[08:51] Samir Das: For forecasting, we're starting small but intend to grow to 10k requests per minute within 6 months if results are good. Would that fit dedicated plans?
[08:59] Jordan Lee: Yes, that's in the realm of Dedicated. We'll include cost/throughput projections.
[09:06] Lena Ortiz: Any known gotchas with cross-region replication or backups? We want logs replicated to our eu-west-1 central logging account only.
[09:14] Jordan Lee: We can route logs to your logging account via Kinesis/Firehose in-region. No cross-region replication unless you request it.
[09:23] Rob Patel: Ok. On timeline, we'd like a pilot starting in late May, run for 2–4 weeks, then evaluate. Is that feasible?
[09:31] Maya Chen: Yes, late May pilot is reasonable. Jordan, are you able to run the bench with their prompts after we get CIDRs and sample prompts?
[09:38] Jordan Lee: Absolutely. We'll need Terraform/CloudFormation permissions or just a diagram to propose the architecture. For Redwood-hosted we can do the provisioning ourselves once approvals are in place.
[09:48] Maya Chen: Great. One more thing: pricing and contract — partly we offer usage pricing for hosted, committed capacity pricing for Dedicated, and a Private licensing model. I'll send a pilot pricing cadence and a high-level contract template.
[10:02] Lena Ortiz: That will help. Any other blockers from your side?
[10:07] Samir Das: No, main blockers are CIDRs, TGW attachment, and security docs.
[10:12] Maya Chen: Perfect. We'll follow up with the docs and set up the technical deep dive for the week of 2026-05-25. Thanks everyone.
[10:22] Lena Ortiz: Thanks.
[10:24] Rob Patel: Thanks all.
[10:26] Emily Nguyen: Bye.

Notes about transcript: occasional mis-heard brand names (we heard "Reedwood" once), filler words like "um" and short crosstalk. Transcript timestamps approximate every few minutes rather than exact 15s marks.
